title: The transformer
lead: This module takes attention apart until you can compute it by hand, differentiate it, tile it the way FlashAttention does and rotate it with RoPE; then it assembles the modern decoder-only block, counts its parameters and FLOPs against published models, and trains a small GPT on a laptop CPU whose loss curve and attention heads you can read.
prerequisites: Module 01: softmax regression, and cross-entropy as the negative log-likelihood of a categorical model

Module 02: backpropagation and the softmax Jacobian diag(p) - p p^T, the softmax/cross-entropy gradient, the activation functions (ReLU, GELU, SiLU), layer normalisation and RMSNorm, AdamW with warmup and cosine decay, gradient clipping, a PyTorch training loop
Module 04: sequence-to-sequence models, Bahdanau and Luong attention, why recurrence is sequential in time
Linear algebra: matrix products and transposes, rank, block-diagonal matrices, 2x2 rotation matrices and orthogonality
Complex numbers: Euler's formula exp(i*phi) = cos(phi) + i sin(phi), the conjugate, and Re(z * conj(w)) as the dot product of two 2D vectors
Probability: expectation and variance of a sum of independent random variables
Python: NumPy arrays and broadcasting; PyTorch tensors, nn.Module and autograd
outcomes: By the end you can compute scaled dot-product attention by hand for a three-token example, with and without a causal mask and with and without the 1/sqrt(d_k) scale, and state every score, weight and output to three decimals.

By the end you can apply the softmax Jacobian diag(p) - p p^T (derived in Module 02) to an attention row, derive the variance argument for 1/sqrt(d_k), and use the two to explain why unscaled attention saturates and learns slowly.
By the end you can push a gradient back through one attention row by hand and check it against autograd.
By the end you can track the shape of every tensor through multi-head and grouped-query attention, from (B, T, d) to (B, h, T, d_k) and back, and explain the residual-stream view of a transformer.
By the end you can write the pre-norm block in equations and code, and explain why it trains stably at depth where post-norm needs a learning-rate warmup.
By the end you can prove that RoPE makes the attention score depend on positions only through t - s, implement it, and verify the property numerically.
By the end you can derive the online softmax and implement tiled (FlashAttention-style) attention that matches naive attention to floating-point rounding without forming the T x T matrix.

By the end you can count the parameters of a decoder from its configuration (12Ld^2 plus embeddings, with GQA and SwiGLU corrections), reproducing published model sizes exactly, and its FLOPs under the convention the whole series uses: 2 N_matmul per token plus 4Ldt for attention at context t (2LdT averaged over a causal sequence of length T), three times that for training, and 6N only as a labelled estimate.
By the end you can compute the KV-cache size per token, in bytes and in KiB, for multi-head, grouped-query and multi-query configurations.

By the end you can train a character-level decoder-only transformer on a CPU, check that its initial loss is log V, sample from it, diagnose a missing causal mask from its loss curve, and find an induction head in a small trained model.
software: PyTorch 2.4 or later (nn.RMSNorm and F.scaled_dot_product_attention); CPU build is enough
Hugging Face transformers (optional, Lab 4 cross-check only; builds models on the meta device, no download)
A GPU is optional throughout; Google Colab is the free option for the GPU part of exercise e15

sections.title: Drop the recurrence
sections.purpose: State the two costs of recurrence that the transformer removes, recast attention as a soft dictionary lookup, and name the two things that must be added back.
must_cover: One-paragraph recap of Module 04: Bahdanau attention computes e_{t,j} = v^T tanh(W_s s_{t-1} + W_h h_j), alpha_{t,j} = softmax_j(e_{t,j}), a_t = sum_j alpha_{t,j} h_j; Luong replaced the score by a dot product s^T W h. Link to Module 04 rather than re-deriving.

The two costs of recurrence, with numbers: (1) step t needs h_{t-1}, so a 10,000-token training sequence is 10,000 dependent steps whatever the hardware; (2) information from position j reaches t through t - j lossy steps. Self-attention: every position attends to every (allowed) position in one matrix multiply, and the path between any two positions is one layer long.

The trade, as a small table from Vaswani et al. (Table 1): per-layer cost O(T d^2) recurrent vs O(T^2 d) self-attention; sequential operations O(T) vs O(1); maximum path length O(T) vs O(1). Self-attention is cheaper per layer when T < d and pays a T^2 price beyond that; forward pointers to Section 10 (FlashAttention, which removes the T^2 memory but not the T^2 arithmetic) and to Module 04's state-space models.

Attention as a soft dictionary lookup. A Python dict returns the value whose key equals the query exactly. Attention scores the query against every key with a dot product, turns the scores into weights with a softmax, and returns the weighted average of the values. Two limits: scaling all scores up makes the softmax approach an argmax (a hard lookup); equal scores give the plain average. Because every step is differentiable, the queries, keys and values can be learned.
What must be added back: order, because a set of weighted sums has no notion of position (Section 6, exercise e4), and for generation a mask that stops a position from seeing its future (Section 2).
worked_examples: Soft lookup with the module's running numbers: query q = (1, 1); keys k1 = (1, 0), k2 = (0, 1), k3 = (1, 1) labelled 'pump', 'valve', 'tank'; values v1 = (1, 0), v2 = (0, 2), v3 = (3, 3). Scores q.k = (1, 1, 2); divided by sqrt(2): (0.707, 0.707, 1.414); softmax weights (0.248, 0.248, 0.503); output 0.248(1,0) + 0.248(0,2) + 0.503(3,3) = (1.759, 2.007). A hard lookup (argmax) would return (3, 3) exactly; equal scores would return the average (1.333, 1.667). Say explicitly that this is row 3 of the worked example in Section 3.

In the soft lookup above, what does the output become if the three scores are equal? -> The plain average of the values, (1.333, 1.667).

sections.title: Scaled dot-product attention
sections.purpose: Define attention exactly, apply the softmax Jacobian (derived in Module 02) to one attention row, derive the variance argument for 1/sqrt(d_k), and define the causal and padding masks.
must_cover: Projections Q = X W_Q, K = X W_K, V = X W_V for X in R^{T x d} (tokens as rows), W_Q, W_K in R^{d x d_k}, W_V in R^{d x d_v}; the roles: a query is what a position looks for, a key what it offers to be matched against, a value what it hands over if matched (source wording).

Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_k)) V. S = Q K^T / sqrt(d_k) is T x T, one score per (query position, key position); softmax along each row; P = softmax(S) has non-negative rows summing to 1; output row i = sum_j P_ij v_j is a convex combination of value rows, so it lies in their convex hull (picture in Section 3).

The softmax Jacobian, recalled in one paragraph with a link to Module 02, Section 3, where it is derived; do not re-derive it here: J = diag(p) - p p^T, entries dp_i/ds_j = p_i (delta_ij - p_j). Name in one clause each the three properties this section uses: every row sums to zero (adding the same constant to all scores leaves p unchanged); J -> 0 as p approaches one-hot; J is largest when p is spread out.

Gradient through one attention row: with g_j = dL/dp_j = (dL/do) . v_j, the chain rule through J gives dL/ds_j = p_j (g_j - sum_k p_k g_k): a key's score is pushed up when its value improves the loss more than the current weighted average does. Section 3 evaluates this with numbers.

Why sqrt(d_k), derived: if the entries of q and k are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, E[q.k] = sum_i E[q_i]E[k_i] = 0 and Var(q.k) = sum_i Var(q_i k_i) = sum_i E[q_i^2] E[k_i^2] = d_k, so the standard deviation is sqrt(d_k): 11.3 at d_k = 128 (the source's 'standard deviation of 11'). Dividing by sqrt(d_k) restores unit variance. State the assumption (unit-variance projections of a normalised input at initialisation) and that training is free to change the scale afterwards.

Connect the two: unscaled scores at d_k = 128 put the softmax in its saturated regime, where J is nearly zero, so the gradients reaching W_Q and W_K are tiny at initialisation. Quote the simulation of Lab 1: d_k = 128, 16 keys, 5,000 draws: unscaled median largest weight 0.978, mean entropy 0.28 nats; scaled median largest weight 0.224, mean entropy 2.36 nats (uniform would be ln 16 = 2.77).
One sentence on QK-normalisation (normalising q and k before the dot product) as a stability device used in some large runs, with a pointer to Module 08; no further detail here.

The causal mask: set S_ij = -inf for j > i before the softmax, so exp(-inf) = 0 exactly and the weights on the future are exactly zero, not small. Training then gives T next-token predictions from one forward pass of a T-token sequence (contrast with Module 04's decoder, which ran step by step even under teacher forcing). Implementation: an additive mask of -inf (or the dtype's most negative finite value) or a boolean mask; PyTorch's is_causal=True.

Padding masks: in a batch of unequal lengths, padded key positions are masked for every query, typically a boolean tensor of shape (B, 1, 1, T) broadcast over heads and query positions; the outputs at padded query positions are computed but meaningless and must be excluded from the loss.

Numerical safety: compute the softmax as exp(s - max(s)) / sum (the overflow example comes in Section 10); a row whose every key is masked divides 0 by 0, so a hand-written softmax returns NaN and some fused kernels return zeros; never rely on either, make sure every query has at least one valid key.
worked_examples: Saturation in numbers: scores (11.3, 0, 0) (a one-standard-deviation gap at d_k = 128, unscaled) give p = (0.999975, 0.000012, 0.000012) and J_11 = p_1(1 - p_1) = 2.5e-5; the scaled scores (1, 0, 0) give p = (0.576, 0.212, 0.212) and J_11 = 0.244, about ten thousand times larger.
Variance check (from Lab 1, 100,000 draws): the standard deviation of q.k is 1.43, 3.99, 7.99 and 11.33 for d_k = 2, 16, 64 and 128, against sqrt(d_k) = 1.41, 4, 8 and 11.31.

checks: Why does the gradient reaching W_Q and W_K almost vanish when one key dominates a row? -> dL/ds = J g with J = diag(p) - p p^T, and J tends to zero as p approaches one-hot, whatever g is.
With d_k = 64 and unit-variance entries, what is the standard deviation of an unscaled score? -> sqrt(64) = 8.
How many entries of a T x T score matrix does a causal mask remove? -> Those with j > i: T(T - 1)/2.

sections.title: The worked example, by hand
sections.purpose: Compute attention on three tokens with and without the mask and the scale, see the outputs as points in the convex hull of the values, and push one gradient back through it.
must_cover: The source's set-up kept exactly: three tokens, d_k = d_v = 2, projected vectors taken directly: Q = K = [[1,0],[0,1],[1,1]], V = [[1,0],[0,2],[3,3]]. Scores QK^T = [[1,0,1],[0,1,1],[1,1,2]]; divided by sqrt(2): [[0.707,0,0.707],[0,0.707,0.707],[0.707,0.707,1.414]].

Causal case, row by row as in the source, with exact three-decimal values: row 1 [1, 0, 0]; row 2 scores [0, 0.707] -> [0.330, 0.670, 0]; row 3 scores [0.707, 0.707, 1.414] -> [0.248, 0.248, 0.503]. Outputs: token 1 (1, 0); token 2 0.330(1,0) + 0.670(0,2) = (0.330, 1.340); token 3 0.248(1,0) + 0.248(0,2) + 0.503(3,3) = (1.759, 2.007). The weights in row 3 sum to 0.999 only because of rounding; say so in a footnote.
The source's interpretation kept: token 3's query (1,1) matched its own key best, and the output is pulled toward its own value.

Unmasked case: row 1 [0.401, 0.198, 0.401] -> (1.604, 1.599); row 2 [0.198, 0.401, 0.401] -> (1.401, 2.006); row 3 unchanged (1.759, 2.007), because the mask removes nothing from the last row. Point out that the weights of rows 1 and 2 mirror each other (swap the first two entries) because Q = K is symmetric under swapping tokens 1 and 2; the outputs differ because v1 and v2 differ.

Unscaled causal case: row 2 [0.269, 0.731] -> (0.269, 1.462); row 3 [0.212, 0.212, 0.576] -> (1.940, 2.152): larger score gaps, sharper weights, outputs pulled further toward the best-matching value. Even at d_k = 2 the effect is visible; at d_k = 128 it is the saturation of Section 2.

Geometry: each output is a convex combination of the value rows it may see, so token 1's output is v1, token 2's lies on the segment v1-v2, token 3's lies inside the triangle v1 v2 v3 (figure). Attention can only mix values; it cannot extrapolate beyond them, which is one reason the FFN and the residual path exist.

The backward pass by hand, causal case, for the scalar L = o_{3,2} (the second component of token 3's output, 2.007): dL/dV has column 2 equal to row 3 of P, (0.248, 0.248, 0.503), and column 1 zero; g_j = v_{j,2} = (0, 2, 3); dL/ds_{3j} = p_j (g_j - 2.007) = (-0.498, -0.002, 0.500), summing to zero as Section 2 promised; dL/dq_3 = sum_j dL/ds_{3j} k_j / sqrt(2) = (0.001, 0.352); dL/dk_j = dL/ds_{3j} q_3 / sqrt(2) = (-0.352, -0.352), (-0.001, -0.001), (0.354, 0.354). Interpretation: raising the second component of q_3 increases its match with keys 2 and 3, whose values have large second components.
Closing paragraph from the source: that is all attention does, a soft, learned lookup; everything else is arranging many of them.

figures.description: Three linked panels. (a) The 3 x 3 scaled score matrix with the three masked cells grey and labelled -inf. (b) The causal weight matrix P as a heat map (sequential single-hue scale 0 to 1) with each cell printed to three decimals. (c) A 2D plot (x from -0.5 to 3.5, y from -0.5 to 3.5) of the value points v1 = (1,0), v2 = (0,2), v3 = (3,3) as labelled dots joined by a light triangle, and the three outputs as hollow markers: o1 = (1, 0) on v1, o2 = (0.330, 1.340) on the segment v1-v2, o3 = (1.759, 2.007) inside the triangle; thin lines from each visible value to o3 with thickness proportional to the weights 0.248, 0.248, 0.503.

checks: Why is token 3's output the same with and without the causal mask? -> The last row is never masked; it already sees every key.
In the unscaled case, why does token 3's output move toward (3, 3)? -> The score gap between key 3 and the others grows from 0.707 to 1, so the softmax puts more weight on v3.
Why must dL/ds_3 sum to zero? -> It is the Jacobian (whose rows sum to zero) applied to g.

sections.title: Multi-head attention and the residual stream
sections.purpose: Run h attentions in parallel with every tensor shape tracked, and read a transformer as a set of layers that read from and write to one shared residual stream.
must_cover: The source formula: MHA(X) = [head_1; ...; head_h] W_O with head_i = Attention(X W_Q^(i), X W_K^(i), X W_V^(i)), d_k = d_v = d/h; with d = 4096 and h = 32 each head works in 128 dimensions (source).

Shape bookkeeping exactly as the source code does it: x (B, T, d) -> wq(x) (B, T, d) -> .view(B, T, h, d_k) -> .transpose(1, 2) (B, h, T, d_k); scores q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) (B, h, T, T); weights @ v (B, h, T, d_k); .transpose(1, 2) (B, T, h, d_k); .reshape(B, T, d) (reshape, not view, because the transpose made the tensor non-contiguous); W_O (B, T, d). All heads are computed by one batched matrix multiply; the head index is just another batch dimension.

Concatenate-then-project equals a sum of per-head writes: [h_1; ...; h_h] W_O = sum_i h_i W_O^(i), where W_O^(i) is the i-th block of d_k rows of W_O. Each head writes its own d_k-dimensional result into the d-dimensional output through its own slice.

Two low-rank circuits per head: the score between positions i and j is x_i W_Q^(i) W_K^(i)T x_j^T / sqrt(d_k), a bilinear form with a d x d matrix of rank at most d_k (the 'QK circuit', deciding where to look); W_V^(i) W_O^(i) is a d x d matrix of rank at most d_k (the 'OV circuit', deciding what to write). Terminology from Elhage et al. (2021).
Why several heads: one softmax gives each query one distribution; h heads let a position attend to several places for different reasons at the same total cost, since h d_k = d.

Counting (source): the four projections are d x d, so 4d^2 parameters per layer; per token the projections cost 8d^2 FLOPs (2 FLOPs per multiply-add), and a token at context t pays 4td for the scores and the mixing (2td for its row of Q K^T, 2td for P V); summed over a sequence the cost is O(T^2 d), quadratic in length. Say that Section 11 turns these counts into the FLOP convention the series uses (with the causal average), and say nothing more about it here.

The residual-stream view: x_0 is the token embedding; every attention layer and every FFN reads from the stream (through a normalisation) and adds its output back; the logits are a linear read-out of the normalised final stream. Layers communicate only through this d-dimensional stream, which is why its width is a shared resource. Forward pointer to Section 5, where the residual connection appears as an equation.

What heads learn, accessibly: a previous-token head attends from t to t - 1; an induction head (Olsson et al. 2022) completes a pattern '... A B ... A -> B' by attending from the current token A to the token that followed the earlier A, which needs two heads in two layers (a previous-token head writes 'the token before me was A' into each position; the induction head's query looks for that). They are a mechanism for copying from context, form fairly abruptly during training, and Lab 6 trains a model in which they appear. Mention the source's examples (matching brackets, the subject of a sentence).

Caution: an attention map shows where information was read from, not why; claims about what a head does need interventions such as zeroing the head and measuring the loss (Lab 6 does this). Cite Jain and Wallace (2019) for the general warning.
worked_examples: Per-head write with numbers: d = 4, h = 2, d_k = 2, head outputs h_1 = (1, 2), h_2 = (0, 1), W_O = I_4. Concatenation gives (1, 2, 0, 1) W_O = (1, 2, 0, 1); the sum of per-head writes gives h_1 W_O[rows 1-2] + h_2 W_O[rows 3-4] = (1, 2, 0, 0) + (0, 0, 0, 1) = (1, 2, 0, 1).

Cost per layer at d = 4,096 for the last token of a 4,096-token context: projections 8d^2 = 134 MFLOP; scores and mixing 4td = 67 MFLOP. Averaged over a causally masked 4,096-token sequence the second figure halves to 34 MFLOP (Section 11).

sections.title: The block: residuals, normalisation and the feed-forward network
sections.purpose: Assemble attention and the feed-forward network into a block, explain why pre-norm trains stably, and say what the feed-forward network contributes.
must_cover: The pre-norm block (source): X <- X + MHA(Norm(X)); X <- X + FFN(Norm(X)). The post-norm block of the original paper: X <- Norm(X + MHA(X)); X <- Norm(X + FFN(X)).

Why pre-norm is stable, written out: unrolling pre-norm gives x_L = x_0 + sum_l F_l(Norm(x_l)), so dx_L/dx_l = I + sum_{m >= l} dF_m/dx_l: an identity path carries the gradient from the loss to every layer untouched. In post-norm every Norm sits on the main path, so the gradient passes through L normalisation Jacobians. Xiong et al. (2020) show that at initialisation the gradients of the parameters near the output of a post-norm transformer are large and do not shrink with depth, while in pre-norm they shrink as depth grows; post-norm therefore needs a learning-rate warmup and diverges without one, pre-norm can train with little or none. Pre-norm has been the standard since about 2020 (source).

Pre-norm's costs: each layer adds to the stream, so its norm grows with depth and later layers change it proportionally less; a final normalisation before the unembedding is required (the code's self.norm). GPT-2 scales the initial weights of the layers that write into the residual stream by 1/sqrt(N), N the number of residual layers, to keep the growth in check.

Normalisation, recalled in one paragraph with a link to Module 02, Section 10, which owns the definitions, the worked examples and the PyTorch modules (do not repeat its examples): LayerNorm(x) = gamma * (x - mean) / std + beta; RMSNorm(x) = gamma * x / sqrt(mean(x^2) + eps), with no mean subtraction and no bias (Zhang and Sennrich 2019), cheaper and as good in transformers. Add the one property this module needs, with its one-line proof: RMSNorm is scale-invariant, RMSNorm(c x) = RMSNorm(x) for c > 0 when eps is negligible, because mean((c x)^2) = c^2 mean(x^2); so each sublayer of a pre-norm block reads only the direction of the residual stream, never its size.

The FFN (source): applied to each position independently, FFN(x) = W_2 phi(W_1 x), inner width d_ff = 4d in the original, 2 x d x 4d = 8d^2 parameters per layer, twice the attention. Attention moves information between positions; the FFN transforms it within a position.

The FFN as a key-value memory (Geva et al. 2021): write FFN(x) = sum_{i=1}^{d_ff} phi(k_i . x) v_i with k_i the i-th row of W_1 and v_i the i-th column of W_2. Each of the d_ff units is a 'memory' that fires when the input matches its key and adds its value direction to the stream. Geva et al. found keys that respond to recognisable input patterns (shallow in lower layers, more semantic in upper ones) and values that raise the probability of plausible next tokens; Meng et al. (2022) located factual associations in mid-layer FFNs. This is why the source says knowledge 'appears to be stored' there: it is an empirical reading, not a design.

SwiGLU (source): FFN_SwiGLU(x) = W_2(SiLU(W_1 x) * W_3 x) with SiLU(z) = z sigmoid(z) (recalled in one clause; SiLU and its comparison with ReLU and GELU are in Module 02, Section 5); the gate multiplies two linear branches elementwise, so each unit can switch its output on, off or negative depending on the input; three matrices, so d_ff ~ (8/3) d keeps 3 x d x (8/3)d = 8d^2. Shazeer (2020) reports lower perplexity for GLU variants than ReLU or GELU FFNs at matched size (quote numbers only from its Table 1).
worked_examples: The growing stream, in numbers sized to a transformer (new; Module 02's small normalisation examples and its activation table are not repeated): RMSNorm(c x) = RMSNorm(x), so a stream that has grown to RMS 8 hands its sublayers the same normalised input as a stream of RMS 1 pointing the same way. Suppose a sublayer writes an update of RMS 1 orthogonal to the stream: a stream of RMS 1 turns by arctan(1/1) = 45 degrees, a stream of RMS 8 by arctan(1/8) = 7.1 degrees. The next RMSNorm passes on only the direction, so the same write moves the grown stream about six times less. This is pre-norm's cost in one line, and the reason for GPT-2's 1/sqrt(N) scaling and the final norm.

SwiGLU width in a real model: d = 4096 gives (8/3)d = 10,922.7, rounded up to a multiple of 256: d_ff = 11,008 (Llama-2-7B). Parameters 3 x 4096 x 11,008 = 135.3M per layer, against 2 x 4096 x 16,384 = 134.2M for a 4d GELU FFN.

In the pre-norm diagram the main line from bottom to top is drawn thick and labelled 'identity path: no Norm on it'; in post-norm the Norm boxes interrupt the thick line.

sections.title: Position
sections.purpose: Inject order into a permutation-equivariant operation, derive RoPE with its complex-number proof, and explain at concept level how a trained context is extended.
must_cover: Permutation equivariance (source): shuffle the input rows and the outputs shuffle with them, because Q, K, V are computed row by row and the softmax is applied per row; the two-line argument here, the full proof in exercise e4. A causal mask breaks the symmetry partly (a position can count how many tokens it sees), so decoder-only models without any positional encoding still learn some position information (Haviv et al. 2022); the encodings below do it deliberately.

Sinusoidal encodings (source formula): PE(t, 2i) = sin(t omega_i), PE(t, 2i+1) = cos(t omega_i), omega_i = 10000^(-2i/d); wavelengths from 2 pi to 2 pi x 10000; added to the token embeddings once at the input. Derive the shift property from the angle-addition formulas: sin((t+k)w) = sin(tw)cos(kw) + cos(tw)sin(kw), cos((t+k)w) = cos(tw)cos(kw) - sin(tw)sin(kw), so each (sin, cos) pair at t + k is a fixed 2 x 2 rotation [[cos kw, sin kw], [-sin kw, cos kw]] of the pair at t: PE(t + k) = M_k PE(t), a linear function independent of t.

Learned absolute embeddings (source): one trained vector per position (GPT-2: 1,024 positions, a 1,024 x 768 table of 786,432 parameters; BERT: 512); nothing exists, or nothing trained exists, beyond the training length, so they cannot extrapolate.

RoPE (source formula): pair the dimensions (q_{2i}, q_{2i+1}) and rotate the pair by t theta_i with theta_i = 10000^(-2i/d_k); the same for keys at their own position s; values are not rotated; applied inside every attention layer, not once at the input.

The complex-number proof, written out: represent a pair as z = x_{2i} + i x_{2i+1}. For two pairs a and b, Re(a conj(b)) = a_x b_x + a_y b_y, their 2D dot product (show the one-line expansion). Rotation by angle phi is multiplication by exp(i phi). So the pair's contribution to the score is Re(z_q exp(i t theta) conj(z_k exp(i s theta))) = Re(z_q conj(z_k) exp(i (t - s) theta)), which depends on t and s only through t - s. Summing over the d_k/2 pairs, q'_t . k'_s depends only on q, k and t - s. Matrix form left to exercise e6.

Properties: no parameters; norms are preserved (rotations are orthogonal); the fast pairs (small i) encode fine position, the slow pairs coarse position; for aligned q and k the score decays on average with distance (the 'long-term decay' of RoFormer), with oscillations.

Wavelengths 2 pi / theta_i: for d_k = 128 and base 10,000 they run from 6.28 tokens to 54,410 tokens; 18 of the 64 pairs have a wavelength longer than 4,096 tokens, so a model trained at 4k context never sees those pairs complete a rotation. These are the pairs that meet unfamiliar angles when the context is extended.

ALiBi (source; Press et al. 2022): no position vectors at all; add -m_h (t - s) to the score of head h; slopes form a geometric sequence, for 8 heads 1/2, 1/4, ..., 1/256; large-slope heads become local, small-slope heads see far; extrapolates beyond the training length at the price of a built-in recency bias.

Context extension, concept level only (source mentions NTK scaling and YaRN): position interpolation (Chen et al. 2023) divides positions by the extension factor kappa = L_target / L_train (written kappa, because s is the key position in this module) so every angle stays inside the trained range, then fine-tunes briefly; NTK-aware scaling raises the base instead, b' = b kappa^(d_k/(d_k - 2)), chosen so that the slowest pair is slowed by exactly kappa while the fastest is unchanged (derive in two lines from theta_last = b^(-(d_k-2)/d_k)); YaRN (Peng et al. 2024) interpolates only the pairs whose wavelength exceeds the trained context, leaves the fast ones alone, ramps between, and adds a small temperature to the logits. Models now also train with a larger base from the start: Llama 3 uses 500,000 (Grattafiori et al. 2024). Pointers: Module 07 (the context window) and Module 08 (long-context mid-training).
worked_examples: RoPE on one pair with theta = 1: q = (1, 0), k = (0, 1). Rotated: q'_t = (cos t, sin t), k'_s = (-sin s, cos s); score = sin t cos s - cos t sin s = sin(t - s). (t, s) = (3, 1): 0.909; (7, 5): 0.909; (1, 3): -0.909; (5, 5): 0. The sign of t - s matters because q is not equal to k.

RoPE on two pairs, d_k = 4, base 10,000 (theta = 1 and 0.01), q = k = (1, 0, 1, 0): score(Delta) = cos(Delta) + cos(0.01 Delta): Delta = 0 -> 2.000; 1 -> 1.540; 2 -> 0.584; 10 -> 0.156; 100 -> 1.403; 300 -> -1.012. The fast pair oscillates every 6.3 tokens; the slow pair varies over hundreds.

Long-term decay, q = k = all ones, d_k = 128, base 10,000, score divided by its value at offset 0 (each pair contributes 2 cos(Delta theta_i), so 128 at offset 0): Delta = 1: 0.970; 16: 0.620; 128: 0.333; 1,024: 0.204; 4,096: -0.053 (Lab 2).
ALiBi, 8 heads, distance 100: head 1 subtracts 50 (weight factor exp(-50) = 2e-22); head 8 subtracts 0.39 (factor 0.68). At distance 1,000 head 8 subtracts 3.9 (factor 0.020).

Panel 2: the same with t = 8, s = 6: both arrows have moved, the angle between them is unchanged. Caption: 'the score sees only the difference'.

A bar per RoPE pair i = 0..63 (d_k = 128) showing log10 of the wavelength 2 pi / theta_i; a horizontal line at 4,096 ('trained context') and one at 16,384 ('target context'). Three overlaid markers per bar: original (base 10^4), position interpolation with kappa = 4 (every bar raised by log10 4), NTK-aware base 40,890 (slow bars raised by up to log10 4, fast bars unchanged). A note that YaRN raises only the bars above the trained-context line.

sections.title: Three shapes of model
sections.purpose: Distinguish encoder-only, decoder-only and encoder-decoder transformers by their masks and objectives, and explain why decoder-only became the default.
must_cover: Encoder-decoder (source; the original model and T5): an encoder reads the input with bidirectional attention; a decoder generates with causal self-attention plus cross-attention, Q = X_dec W_Q, K = H_enc W_K, V = H_enc W_V, score shape (B, h, T_dec, T_enc). Cross-attention has no causal mask (the whole input is known before decoding starts), only a padding mask on encoder positions; the encoder's K and V are computed once per input and reused at every decoding step. Each decoder layer has three sublayers, so 16d^2 parameters against an encoder layer's 12d^2. Uses: translation, summarisation (source).

Encoder-only (source; BERT): bidirectional attention, trained by masked language modelling: 15% of positions are selected, of which 80% are replaced by [MASK], 10% by a random token and 10% left unchanged, and the loss is taken on the selected positions only. Produces contextual representations (a [CLS] vector or mean-pooled states) for classification, retrieval and embeddings; cannot generate (exercise e8). BERT-Base: 12 layers, d = 768, 110M parameters.
Decoder-only (source; GPT): causal attention, next-token loss at every position; generates; with enough scale does the other shapes' tasks by being prompted (source).
The prefix LM in one sentence: bidirectional attention over a prompt, causal over the continuation; a middle ground explored in the T5 study.

Why decoder-only won, with the source's reasons expanded and each supported: every position is a training target (T - 1 targets per sequence against about 15% for masked LM); one objective and one architecture cover every task once the task is written as text (GPT-2's zero-shot and GPT-3's few-shot results; in-context learning is Module 07); generation is the task people want (source); one stack and one KV cache (Section 9) over prompt and answer make serving simple; the scaling-law evidence of Module 07 was gathered on this shape.

The honest counterpoint: in controlled comparisons the answer depends on the evaluation. Raffel et al. (2020) found an encoder-decoder with a denoising objective best at equal compute for fine-tuned tasks; Wang et al. (2022) found a causal decoder trained on plain next-token prediction best for zero-shot use straight after pretraining. Generality and simplicity won the market. Encoders remain the efficient choice for embeddings and retrieval; cross-link to the AI Agents series (retrieval-augmented generation) for how they are used.
The masks are the cleanest way to tell the shapes apart (figure): full square (encoder), lower triangle (decoder), full rectangle T_dec x T_enc (cross-attention).
worked_examples: The original base model from this module's counts: d = 512, d_ff = 2,048 = 4d, 6 encoder + 6 decoder layers. Encoder layer 12d^2 = 3.15M; decoder layer 16d^2 = 4.19M; layers total 6 x 3.15M + 6 x 4.19M = 44.0M; one embedding matrix shared by encoder input, decoder input and output projection, about 37,000 x 512 = 18.9M; total about 63M against the 65M the paper reports (Table 3). The remaining 3% is not itemised in the paper; say so rather than inventing a reason.
Training signal from one 512-token sequence: decoder-only 511 next-token targets; BERT about 77 (15% of 512).

figures.description: Three columns titled 'encoder-only (BERT)', 'decoder-only (GPT)', 'encoder-decoder (T5, the original)'. Each shows a block stack and beneath it its attention mask(s) as 6 x 6 grids with allowed cells filled: encoder full square; decoder lower triangle; encoder-decoder shows the encoder's full square, the decoder's lower triangle, and the cross-attention's full 5 x 6 rectangle (decoder queries by encoder keys). Under each column, its training objective in one line: 'fill in masked tokens', 'predict the next token', 'map input to output text'. A small inset shows the prefix-LM mask (full over the first three positions, causal after).

sections.title: The vision transformer
sections.purpose: Show that nothing in the transformer is specific to text: an image becomes a sequence of patch tokens.
must_cover: Patches as tokens (Dosovitskiy et al. 2021): a 224 x 224 x 3 image cut into 16 x 16 patches gives 14 x 14 = 196 patches; each is flattened to 16 x 16 x 3 = 768 numbers and mapped to width d by one linear layer (equivalently a convolution with kernel 16 and stride 16); a learned [CLS] token is prepended (197 tokens); learned position embeddings are added; an encoder-only stack follows; the class is read from the final [CLS] vector.

ViT-Base/16 counted with Section 11's rules: 12 layers, d = 768, 12 heads, MLP 3,072; transformer body 12Ld^2 = 84.9M (85.1M with biases and norms), patch embedding 768 x 768 + 768 = 590,592 parameters (0.59M; this module owns the worked example, and Module 03 points here rather than repeating it), positions 197 x 768 = 0.15M, a 1,000-class head 0.77M: about 86M, as published.

Inductive bias: no locality or translation equivariance is built in (contrast Module 03's convolutions), so a ViT must learn them from data; trained on ImageNet-sized data alone it trails comparable CNNs, and it needs large-scale pretraining, or strong augmentation and distillation (DeiT, Touvron et al. 2021), to match or beat them.
Cost: tokens grow with the square of the resolution and attention with the square of the tokens, so doubling the resolution multiplies the attention cost per layer by about 16.
Where it is used: CLIP's image encoder (Module 05); multimodal language models project a vision encoder's patch outputs into the token stream (Module 07).
worked_examples: Tokens at 224 x 224: 197; at 448 x 448: 28 x 28 + 1 = 785. Score entries per head per layer: 197^2 = 38,809 versus 785^2 = 616,225, a factor of 15.9.

sections.title: The modern decoder block, part by part
sections.purpose: Walk through the choices in a current open decoder layer and the reason for each, introducing the KV cache that grouped-query attention exists to shrink.
must_cover: The source's table kept verbatim (component / choice / reason): normalisation RMSNorm pre-norm (stable at depth, cheaper than layer norm); position RoPE (relative, parameter-free, extendable); attention grouped-query; activation SwiGLU (better loss at equal parameters than ReLU/GELU FFNs); biases none (marginal; removed for stability and simplicity); attention kernel FlashAttention. Each row points to the section that justified it (5, 6, this section, 5, this section, 10).

The KV cache (key-value cache), introduced only (depth in Module 10): when a model generates, each new token's query must attend to the keys and values of every earlier token in every layer; storing them avoids recomputing the whole prefix at every step. Size per token: bytes = 2 x L x n_kv x d_head x bytes per value (the 2 is K and V). State the module's unit convention here, at its first size in bytes, once: sizes computed from tensor shapes are given in binary units (1 KiB = 1,024 B, 1 MiB = 2^20 B, 1 GiB = 2^30 B), quoted hardware figures in the vendor's decimal units (GB, TB/s), and a size that recurs in Modules 07-10, which work in decimal GB, is given in both forms.

Grouped-query attention (source; Ainslie et al. 2023): keep all h query heads but give each group of h / n_kv query heads one shared key-value head; the cache and the K and V projections shrink by the group size, with quality close to full multi-head attention; 8 query heads per KV head is common (source). Multi-query attention (Shazeer 2019) is the extreme, one KV head. Ainslie et al. also show how to convert ('uptrain') an existing multi-head checkpoint. The FLOPs of Q K^T do not change: every query head still scores every key.

How the code shares heads: k.repeat_interleave(h // n_kv, dim=1), so query heads 0-3 use KV head 0 and 4-7 use KV head 1 when h = 8 and n_kv = 2; repeat (which would give 0, 1, 0, 1, ...) is the classic bug, silent because the shapes still match (source's failure mode).

No biases, and tied embeddings: the source code ties the input embedding to the output projection, common in small models where the V x d matrix is a large share (Section 11); large models often untie.

Sliding-window attention (source): each position attends only to the last w positions, cost O(Tw) instead of O(T^2); with a window of w positions including itself, each layer extends the reach by w - 1, so L layers reach back about L w (the source's 'effective receptive field'). Mistral 7B used w = 4,096 with 32 layers, a theoretical span of about 131k tokens (Jiang et al. 2023). The KV cache becomes a rolling buffer of w entries per layer. Used alone or alternated with full-attention layers (source). One sentence on attention sinks: models put large weight on the first few tokens, so a streaming window that evicts them degrades; keeping those few tokens' keys and values fixes it (Xiao et al. 2024).
FlashAttention in one paragraph (source): the same attention, computed in tiles without storing the T x T matrix; the derivation is the next section.
What has not changed since 2017: the attention formula and the residual structure. Everything in the table is a refinement of Sections 2-6.
worked_examples: KV cache per token in bf16 with L = 32 and d_head = 128: multi-head (32 KV heads, the Llama-2-7B layout) 2 x 32 x 32 x 128 x 2 B = 524,288 B (512 KiB); GQA with 8 KV heads (the Llama-3-8B layout) 131,072 B (128 KiB); MQA 16,384 B (16 KiB). For one 4,096-token sequence: 2 GiB (2.15 GB), 512 MiB (0.54 GB), 64 MiB (0.067 GB). Module 10 repeats the calculation for the case-study model, in decimal units.
Head mapping with h = 8, n_kv = 2: repeat_interleave gives KV heads [0,0,0,0,1,1,1,1] for query heads 0..7; repeat would give [0,1,0,1,0,1,0,1].
Sliding window w = 4 on T = 8: position 7 sees positions 4-7 in layer 1; through 3 layers it reaches back 3 x (4 - 1) = 9 positions, so every earlier position.

sections.title: FlashAttention and the online softmax
sections.purpose: Derive the online softmax and show how it lets attention be computed exactly in tiles, without storing the T x T matrix.
must_cover: Why standard attention is limited by memory traffic, not arithmetic, on a GPU (source): implemented as three steps it writes S (T x T) to the GPU's main memory (HBM), reads it back for the softmax, writes P, reads P back for P V. The softmax does a handful of FLOPs per element it moves. On an A100, HBM moves 1.5-2.0 TB/s while on-chip SRAM (192 KB per streaming multiprocessor, 108 of them) moves about 19 TB/s (figures as quoted by Dao et al. 2022, Section 2.1); dense bf16 arithmetic peaks at 312 TFLOP/s (NVIDIA's specification for the A100). The roofline model that makes this precise is in Module 10.
The size that hurts: for T = 8,192 and h = 32 in bf16, S for one layer is 32 x 8,192^2 x 2 B = 4 GiB, and a backward pass would need P for every layer.

Safe softmax: exp(s - m) / sum exp(s - m) with m = max(s) gives the same result and cannot overflow (the example: softmax of (1000, 1001, 1002) computed naively is NaN; safely, (0.090, 0.245, 0.665)). It needs the maximum before the sum: two passes over the scores.

Online softmax (Milakov and Gimelshein 2018), derived: keep a running maximum m and a running sum l = sum exp(s_j - m) over the scores seen so far. When a block with maximum m_b and local sum l_b = sum_{j in block} exp(s_j - m_b) arrives: m' = max(m, m_b); l' = l exp(m - m') + l_b exp(m_b - m'). Proof by induction that after the last block l = sum_j exp(s_j - m_final): each stored term exp(s_j - m) becomes exp(s_j - m') after multiplying by exp(m - m').

The same trick for the output: keep an unnormalised accumulator a = sum exp(s_j - m) v_j; on a new block a' = a exp(m - m') + sum_{j in block} exp(s_j - m') v_j; at the end the output is a / l, which equals sum_j softmax(s)_j v_j. One pass, no stored scores.

The tiled algorithm (Dao et al. 2022, Algorithm 1, in words): split Q into row blocks of B_r rows and K, V into blocks of B_c rows; for each query block, loop over key/value blocks, compute the B_r x B_c tile of scores in SRAM, update m, l and a per row as above, discard the tile; write the output block once. Under a causal mask, tiles entirely above the diagonal are skipped (about half). Extra memory is O(T) (m and l per row) instead of O(T^2) (source).

The backward pass recomputes instead of storing: keep only the per-row log-sum-exp (m + log l) and recompute each tile of S and P when it is needed; more FLOPs, far fewer bytes, faster overall (source's 'several-fold').

Exact, not approximate: the same arithmetic in a different order, equal up to floating-point rounding (Lab 3: 5.6e-16 in float64, 3.4e-7 in float32). Contrast sliding-window or sparse attention, which change the function (exercise e10).

Descendants in one sentence each: FlashAttention-2 (Dao 2024) parallelises better over the sequence; later versions target newer GPUs; PyTorch's F.scaled_dot_product_attention dispatches to a fused kernel when the inputs allow (the source code's comment); paged attention is serving, Module 10.

sections.title: Counting parameters and FLOPs
sections.purpose: Derive a decoder's parameter count and per-token compute from its configuration, check the formulas against published models, and fix the FLOP convention that the rest of the series links to.
must_cover: Per layer (source): attention 4d^2 with full multi-head attention, 2d^2 + 2 d n_kv d_head with GQA; FFN 8d^2 (2 x d x 4d, or 3 x d x (8/3)d for SwiGLU); norms 2d, negligible; total about 12d^2, so about 12 L d^2 for L layers.
Embeddings (source): V x d, twice if the output projection is not tied to the input; plus T_max x d for learned positions if any.

The source's check on the Llama 7B layout, made exact: d = 4,096, L = 32, 32 heads (multi-head), d_ff = 11,008, V = 32,000, untied. Per layer 67,108,864 (attention) + 135,266,304 (FFN) + 8,192 (norms) = 202,383,360; x 32 = 6,476,267,520; embeddings 2 x 32,000 x 4,096 = 262,144,000; final norm 4,096; total 6,738,415,616, the published 6.7B. The rule 12Ld^2 + 2Vd gives 6.44B + 0.26B = 6.70B, within 0.6% (source's 'about 6.7 billion').

Small models are different (table from Lab 4): GPT-2 small 124,439,808, SmolLM2-135M 134,515,008, Qwen2.5-0.5B 494,032,768, Llama-2-7B 6,738,415,616, Llama-3-8B 8,030,261,248, each matching its published size; the embedding share is 32%, 21%, 28%, 3.9% and 13%; the non-embedding count differs from 12Ld^2 by factors 1.00, 0.89, 1.55, 1.005 and 1.08 because of GQA and FFN width. Count from the configuration, not from the rule.

Two parameter counts, named here once for the whole series: N_total, every parameter, which sets memory (bytes = N_total x bytes per value) and is the N of the scaling laws (Module 07); and N_matmul, the parameters that take part in a matrix multiply for every token, which is N_total minus the lookup tables: an untied input embedding (V d) and any learned position table. Norm gains and biases stay in (they are negligible). With tied embeddings the shared V x d matrix counts once in both, because it is used once, as the output head. Llama-2-7B: N_total = 6,738,415,616 and N_matmul = 6,607,343,616.

FLOPs: a product of an (m x n) and an (n x p) matrix costs 2mnp FLOPs (one multiply and one add per term). Per token each parameter in N_matmul takes part in one multiply-add, so the matrix multiplies cost 2 N_matmul FLOPs per token; the input embedding is a lookup and costs nothing, while the output projection costs 2Vd even when tied. Attention adds, per layer, 2td for a token's row of Q K^T and 2td for mixing the values when the token sits at context t (it attends to t positions; h d_head = d, and GQA does not change this): 4Ldt per token. Over a causally masked sequence of length T, t runs from 1 to T, so the average is 4Ld(T + 1)/2, about 2LdT per token. This assumes the kernel skips the masked half, as FlashAttention's causal tiling does (Section 10); a kernel that computes the full T x T square pays 4LdT per token. 2LdT is the form in Kaplan et al. (2020).

The crossover, derived: for one token at context t, attention equals the matrix multiplies when 4Ldt = 2 x 12Ld^2, that is at t = 6d: 24,576 tokens for d = 4,096 and 4,608 for d = 768; averaged over a causal sequence the crossing moves to T = 12d. This is why 2N is the rule of thumb 'until the context gets long' (source).

Training costs three times the forward pass, derived (this module owns the derivation; Module 02 keeps only the argument that the backward pass costs about twice the forward, and Modules 07, 08 and 10 link here): for a layer Y = XW the forward pass is one product; the backward pass needs dX = dY W^T and dW = X^T dY, each the size of the forward product; the input embedding's backward is a scatter-add of d numbers per token, negligible. So training costs 6 N_matmul + 12Ldt per token at context t, or 6 N_matmul + 6LdT per token averaged over a causal sequence, and C = (6 N_matmul + 6LdT) D for D training tokens. The familiar C = 6ND, with N = N_total and no attention term, is an estimate: quote it only labelled as one, with its error (for Llama-2-7B at T = 4,096 it is 5.7% low). Planning a budget with it is Module 08; fitting the Chinchilla law is Module 07.

The convention, as one boxed summary that Modules 02, 07, 08 and 10 link to instead of restating it: (1) memory and the scaling-law N use N_total; (2) forward FLOPs per token are 2 N_matmul + 4Ldt at context t, which averages to 2 N_matmul + 2LdT over a causal sequence of length T; (3) the input embedding is excluded because it is a lookup; (4) training costs three times the forward pass; (5) 2 N_total and 6 N_total may be quoted only as labelled estimates.

Memory per parameter, one line as a preview: weights take N_total x bytes per value; Llama-2-7B in bf16 is 6,738,415,616 x 2 B = 13.5 GB (12.6 GiB), given in both units because Modules 07-10 quote weights in decimal GB. Full accounting of optimiser states and activations is Module 08, of inference memory Module 10.
worked_examples: Llama-2-7B, exact: N_total = 6,738,415,616 parameters, as itemised above; removing the 131,072,000-parameter input embedding leaves N_matmul = 6,607,343,616.

Llama-2-7B forward FLOPs per token: 2 N_matmul = 13.21 GFLOP for the matrix multiplies. Attention for one token at context t = 512, 4,096 and 32,768 (4Ldt): 0.27, 2.15 and 17.18 GFLOP, that is 2%, 14% and 57% of that token's total (or +2%, +16% and +130% on top of the matrix multiplies). Averaged over a causally masked 4,096-token training sequence (2LdT): 1.07 GFLOP, +8%. The +16% applies to the last token of a 4,096-token context, or to a kernel that computes the masked half; a training sequence pays +8%.

The source's tiny decoder (V = 4,096, d = 256, 4 layers, 8 heads, 2 KV heads, d_ff = 682, tied): 3,801,344 parameters, against 12Ld^2 = 3,145,728 plus 1,048,576 of embeddings; exercise e12 itemises it.

Training Llama-2-7B, per token at T = 4,096, under the convention: 6 N_matmul = 39.64 GFLOP plus 6LdT = 3.22 GFLOP, 42.87 GFLOP in all. The quick 6 N_total = 40.43 GFLOP is 5.7% low: it counts the input embedding (0.79 GFLOP that is never spent) and leaves out attention (3.22 GFLOP). Exercise e13 turns this into a compute budget and a utilisation.

checks: Why does a tied embedding still cost 2Vd FLOPs per token? -> The output projection is still computed; tying shares the parameters, not the arithmetic.
For one token at context t in a model with d = 768, at what t does attention cost as much as the matrix multiplies, by the 12Ld^2 rule? -> t = 6d = 4,608 tokens.

Why does a causally masked training sequence pay about half the attention FLOPs per token that its last token pays? -> Position t attends to t keys, and t averages (T + 1)/2 over the sequence, provided the kernel skips the masked entries.

sections.title: Training a tiny GPT
sections.purpose: Walk through the eighty-line decoder, train it at character level on a CPU, sample from it, and read its loss curve, including the curve of a model with the mask removed.
must_cover: The source code, kept (with one added line, below), toured against the sections: rope() (Section 6), Attention with GQA via repeat_interleave (Sections 4 and 9), F.scaled_dot_product_attention(..., is_causal=True) (Sections 2 and 10), Block with pre-norm and SwiGLU (Section 5), Decoder with tied embeddings and a final RMSNorm (Sections 5 and 11). The printed parameter count is 3,801,344 (source's '~3.8M').

The loss at initialisation should be log V: with small weights the logits are nearly equal, the softmax nearly uniform, and the cross-entropy -log(1/V) = log V; slightly more in practice, about log V + sigma^2/2 for logits with a small standard deviation sigma. For V = 4,096, log V = 8.318.

The added line, told as a lesson: nn.Embedding initialises its weights N(0, 1), and the output projection shares them, so the final normalised state of position t, which still resembles its own input embedding, has a dot product of about d = 256 with that embedding. The model as first written predicts its current token with a logit near 236 and starts at a loss of 231, not 8.3. Initialising the embedding with standard deviation 0.02 (GPT-2's choice) gives 8.33-8.45 across seeds. Rule: check the step-0 loss against log V before training anything.
Inputs and targets: tokens[:, :-1] predict tokens[:, 1:] (the shift); every position is a training example; a batch is a set of random windows of T + 1 characters.

The corpus of Lab 5: a generated plant-maintenance log, one record per line, e.g. 'P-104 pump pressure 4.2 bar OK end P-104', in which the status follows from the value and the identifier at the end repeats the one at the start. Reference levels in nats per character: log V = 3.829 (V = 46); unigram entropy 3.410; bigram conditional entropy 1.717; the generator's true entropy 0.330; and 0.500 if the repeated identifier is treated as unpredictable. Each number is computed in the lab.

Training (the loop of Module 02): AdamW with beta = (0.9, 0.95) and weight decay 0.1, learning rate 3e-3 with 50 warmup steps and cosine decay, gradient clipping at 1.0, batches of 32 windows of 128 characters; a 0.73M-parameter model (d = 128, 4 layers, 4 heads, 2 KV heads).

Sampling: feed a newline, take the last position's logits, divide by a temperature (0.8 here; decoding strategies are Module 07), sample, append, crop the context to the last 128 characters, repeat. Without a KV cache every step recomputes the whole window; the cache of Section 9 removes that, and Module 10 builds it.

Reading the curve: the loss falls through the unigram and bigram levels within about 100 steps and flattens near 0.5: the model has the format, the vocabulary and the status rule, and treats the closing identifier as unpredictable. Getting below 0.5 requires copying the identifier from about 35 characters back, which is an induction-style mechanism (Section 4, Lab 6). Lab 5's FULL run (1,500 steps) shows that step happening: after about 1,000 steps on the plateau the loss drops within about 200 steps to about 0.40, and from then on almost every sampled line closes with the identifier it opened with. When the drop comes is not reproducible to the step: it depends on the learning-rate schedule and even on the machine's arithmetic (prototype runs of the same 1,500-step schedule on 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 CPU threads began the drop anywhere between steps 600 and 1,000, and all ended at 0.395-0.397), and a schedule that is too short can end in the middle of it (a 1,300-step schedule stopped at 0.44 with 14% of identifiers copied). That the drop is abrupt when it comes is the robust part. The remaining gap to 0.330 is the value distributions, which the model has not learned exactly.

Removing the mask (source): retrain with is_causal=False and the training loss falls to about 0.02 within 150-200 steps, because every position can read its target through attention; the validation loss falls just as far, because the leak is in the architecture, not in the data split; samples are garbage; scoring each next character from its prefix alone (as generation does) gives 1.27 nats for the leaky model against 0.53 for the causal model after QUICK and 0.40 after FULL (both settings train the unmasked model for the same 200 steps); the leaky model still beats the bigram level only because the last position of each training window cannot see its target. The off-by-one shift bug produces a similar too-good curve (source).
worked_examples: Initial loss: V = 4,096: log V = 8.318; the code as first written prints 231.4 (seed 0), 236.2 and 239.5 (seeds 1, 2); with the 0.02 initialisation 8.39, 8.33, 8.45. Lab corpus: V = 46, log V = 3.829, observed 3.884 at step 0.

Recomputation without a cache: generating 128 characters from a single newline reprocesses the whole prefix each step, 1 + 2 + ... + 128 = 8,256 position-forwards, against 128 with a KV cache, a factor of 64.5.

Solid line: the causal model from the FULL run, starting at 3.88, crossing the unigram and bigram levels within 100 steps, sitting between 0.52 and 0.57 until about step 1,000, dropping to 0.40 by step 1,200 and ending at 0.397 (validation) at step 1,500; dashed line: the same model trained without the causal mask for 200 steps, plunging to 0.024 (validation) by step 150 and 0.019 at step 200. checks: A model with V = 256 reports a loss of 12.7 at step 0. What do you check first? -> The scale of the initial logits (embedding and output-projection initialisation), since log 256 = 5.55.
Why does a validation set not reveal a missing causal mask? -> The leak is present on every split; only generation or prefix-only scoring exposes it.

what_goes_wrong: Training and validation loss collapse to near zero within a few hundred steps and generation is garbage -> the causal mask is missing, or the target shift is off by one, so each position reads its answer -> restore is_causal=True and the tokens[:, :-1] / tokens[:, 1:] shift; test by changing token t + 1 and checking that the logits at position t do not change, or by prefix-only scoring (Lab 5: 1.27 against 0.53 nats).

The loss at step 0 is far above log V (231 instead of 8.3 for V = 4,096) -> the logits are large at initialisation; a tied embedding initialised N(0, 1) makes each position predict its own token -> initialise the embedding with standard deviation 0.02 or scale the logits; always compare the step-0 loss with log V.
A deep post-norm model diverges in the first hundred steps -> large gradients near the output at initialisation (Xiong et al. 2020) -> use pre-norm, or a learning-rate warmup.

The loss becomes inf or NaN at long contexts in fp16 -> scores overflow fp16's maximum of 65,504 (with entries of q and k around 30, the 128 products of 900 each already sum to 115,200) -> use bf16, compute the softmax in fp32, or normalise q and k.

A RoPE model trains worse than expected and extrapolates badly -> RoPE was applied to the values, or to only one of q and k, so the score is no longer a function of t - s (Lab 2: diagonal deviation about 11 instead of 2e-14) -> rotate exactly q and k, with the same positions.

A converted checkpoint produces fluent-looking nonsense -> RoPE pairing conventions differ (adjacent pairs, as in the code here, versus the first and second halves of the head dimension in other implementations), so q and k are rotated with the wrong partners -> permute the q and k projection rows to match the convention, and compare one layer's scores with the reference implementation.

Long-context quality degrades in a model computed in bf16 -> positions or angles were computed in bf16, where positions 4,090 to 4,099 all round to 4,096, so neighbouring tokens get identical rotations -> compute positions and angles in fp32.
Batched generation continues from padding -> sequences were right-padded for a causal model -> left-pad for generation and pass the attention mask and correct position ids.

A model degrades slowly and confusingly as it generates -> positions in the KV cache were miscounted after the prompt, so RoPE angles are wrong for generated tokens -> the position of a generated token is the prompt length plus the number generated so far (Module 10).

Grouped-query attention costs quality with no error message -> KV heads repeated in the wrong order (repeat instead of repeat_interleave), so query heads use another group's keys -> unit-test against the ungrouped case by copying weights into a model with n_kv = h.

NaN appears for some sequences in a padded batch -> a query row has every key masked, and the softmax divides 0 by 0 -> make sure every query has at least one valid key, or zero those rows explicitly.

Perplexity explodes beyond the training length -> RoPE angles for the slow pairs, or absolute positions, were never seen in training -> apply position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling or YaRN with a short fine-tune, or stay within the trained length.

A head is declared to 'do' something because its attention map looks like it -> attention weights show where information was read, not what it was used for -> test with an intervention: zero the head and measure the loss (Lab 6).

labs.goal: Reproduce every number of the worked example in NumPy, confirm them with PyTorch's fused attention and autograd, and measure the effect of the 1/sqrt(d_k) scale.
labs.data: Synthetic: the worked example's 3 x 2 matrices, and standard-normal random vectors (numpy.random.default_rng(0)).
steps: Define Q = K = [[1,0],[0,1],[1,1]] and V = [[1,0],[0,2],[3,3]] as float64 arrays; write softmax(s) with max subtraction and attention(Q, K, V, causal=True, scale=True) that returns S, P, O, masking with -inf where j > i. Print S, P and O for the causal scaled case: P row 2 = [0.330 0.670 0.000], row 3 = [0.248 0.248 0.503]; O = [[1.000 0.000] [0.330 1.340] [1.759 2.007]].

Every output row is a convex combination of the value rows it may see; with the mask, row 1 is exactly v1 whatever Q and K are.

labs.goal: Implement rotary position embedding, verify numerically that scores depend only on relative position, see what breaks it, and look at wavelengths, long-term decay, interpolation and ALiBi.
labs.data: Synthetic: hand-chosen and random query and key vectors (numpy.random.default_rng(0), torch.manual_seed(0)).
steps: Write rope_np(x, positions, base=10000.0) for arrays of shape (n, d) that rotates adjacent pairs (x[..., 0::2], x[..., 1::2]) by position x theta_i, theta_i = base^(-2i/d), exactly as the module's torch rope(). Print the one-pair example with theta = 1, q = (1, 0), k = (0, 1): scores 0.909 at (3, 1), 0.909 at (7, 5), -0.909 at (1, 3), 0.000 at (5, 5).

Place one random q and one random k (d = 64) at every position 0..63, build the 64 x 64 score matrix, and print the largest deviation of any diagonal from its own mean: about 2e-14 in float64. The matrix is Toeplitz: the score depends only on t - s.
Print the change in vector norm after rotation (about 1e-15): rotations preserve length.
Break it: rotate only q and rebuild the matrix; the diagonal deviation jumps to about 11.

Check the module's torch rope() against complex multiplication (torch.view_as_complex on adjacent pairs times torch.polar(1, angle)): maximum difference about 2e-7 in float32. Repeat the Toeplitz test in float32 at T = 256: deviation about 4e-5, the rounding of large angles in single precision.

Long-term decay: q = k = ones(128); compute the score divided by its value at offset 0 (128) for offsets 1 to 16,384 for base 10,000 and 500,000; print selected values for base 10,000 (1: 0.970, 16: 0.620, 128: 0.333, 1,024: 0.204, 4,096: -0.053) and plot both curves on a log x-axis (fig-06-13).
Wavelengths for d = 128: print the fastest and slowest (6.28 and 54,410 tokens for base 10,000) and the number of pairs longer than 4,096 tokens (18 of 64 for base 10,000; 32 for base 500,000).
Position interpolation: compute the score matrix for 256 positions with positions divided by 4, and confirm that its entries at multiples of 4 equal the original 64 x 64 matrix (difference 0.0).

ALiBi: build the bias tensor -m_h max(0, t - s) for 8 heads and T = 6; print head 1's matrix (steps of -0.5 below the diagonal) and the slopes [0.5 0.25 0.125 0.0625 0.03125 0.015625 0.0078125 0.00390625].
