Fast pairs wrap every few tokens, slow pairs barely turn within thousands; the score for aligned q and k decays with distance on average, with oscillations.
Position interpolation maps a longer range of positions onto angles already seen in training, which is why it needs only a short fine-tune.
extensions: Compute the NTK-aware base for kappa = 4 (40,890) and plot the 64 wavelengths before and after on a log scale with a line at 4,096.
Implement the 'rotate half' convention (pair dimension i with i + d/2) and show it also gives a Toeplitz matrix but different numbers for the same q and k: the source of checkpoint-conversion bugs.
Add RoPE to Lab 1's attention and confirm that shifting all positions by the same amount leaves every output unchanged.

labs.title: Online softmax and tiled attention
labs.goal: Implement the online softmax and a FlashAttention-style tiled forward pass in NumPy, and show they equal the naive computation while never holding more than one tile of scores.
labs.data: Synthetic: random scores and random Q, K, V (numpy.random.default_rng(0)); the worked example.
steps: Naive versus safe softmax on (1000, 1001, 1002): the naive version overflows and prints [nan nan nan] (silence NumPy's warning with np.errstate); the safe version prints [0.090 0.245 0.665].

Write online_softmax_stats(s) that streams once through s keeping (m, l) with the update m' = max(m, s_j), l' = l exp(m - m') + exp(s_j - m'). On 10,000 scores drawn with standard deviation 5, turn (m, l) into probabilities and compare with the safe softmax: maximum difference about 9e-16.

Trace row 3 of the worked example with blocks of two keys, printing m, l and the accumulator after each block: after block 1 m = 0.707, l = 2.000, a = [1, 2]; after block 2 m = 1.414, rescale 0.493, l = 1.986, a = [3.493, 3.986]; output a / l = [1.759, 2.007].

Write tiled_attention(Q, K, V, Br=64, Bc=64, causal=True) following Algorithm 1: outer loop over query blocks; per row running m, l and accumulator; inner loop over key/value blocks, stopping at the diagonal block when causal and masking inside it; output acc / l. On T = 1,024, d = 64 float64 inputs, print the maximum difference from naive attention (about 5.6e-16), the same in float32 against the float64 reference (about 3.4e-7, the same as naive float32), and unmasked (about 1.7e-16).
Print the bookkeeping: tiles computed 136 of 256 under the causal mask; the largest score block held 64 x 64 x 8 B = 32 KiB, against 1,024^2 x 8 B = 8 MiB for the naive score matrix.
Run the worked example through tiled_attention with Br = 1, Bc = 2 and confirm it prints [[1, 0], [0.330, 1.340], [1.759, 2.007]].

Time both functions once and remark that on a CPU in NumPy the timing says nothing about a GPU: the benefit of tiling is fewer bytes moved between HBM and on-chip memory, which this lab counts rather than measures.
expected_observations: The online and tiled computations equal the naive ones to rounding error; reordering the arithmetic changes nothing that matters.
The rescaling factor exp(m - m') is the only new idea; dropping it (try it) gives wrong outputs whenever a later block holds a larger score.
Under a causal mask about half the tiles are never computed, and memory for scores stays at one tile however long the sequence.
extensions: Implement the backward pass by recomputation: store only the log-sum-exp per row, recompute each tile of P, and check dQ, dK, dV against PyTorch autograd on T = 128.
Use unequal tiles (Br = 32, Bc = 128) and confirm the output does not change.

Count element reads and writes of Q, K, V, S, P and O for the naive and tiled versions as a function of an assumed on-chip capacity M, and compare with the Theta(T d + T^2) and Theta(T^2 d^2 / M) of Dao et al.

labs.title: A parameter and FLOP counter for Llama-style models
labs.goal: Write a counter for decoder parameters, FLOPs under Section 11's convention and KV-cache size from a configuration, and check it against PyTorch, against the module's Decoder and against five published models.
labs.data: Configurations of published models hard-coded in the lab from their config.json files (no download); optional cross-check with transformers on PyTorch's meta device (no download, no memory).
steps: Write a dataclass Cfg(name, V, d, L, h, n_kv, d_ff, tied, glu=True, bias='none'|'qkv'|'all', learned_pos=0, norm_bias=False) and count(cfg) returning a dict with embeddings, per-layer attention, per-layer MLP, norms, the total (N_total) and n_matmul (the total minus an untied input embedding and any learned position table), following Section 11.
Check it against the module's Decoder built in PyTorch: both give 3,801,344.

Optional cross-check: build each Llama-family configuration with transformers.LlamaConfig and LlamaForCausalLM inside 'with torch.device("meta"):' (and Qwen2Config/Qwen2ForCausalLM, GPT2Config()/GPT2LMHeadModel) and sum p.numel(): identical counts, built in seconds without allocating weights.

Write flops_per_token(cfg, t, causal_avg=False, train=False) implementing Section 11's convention: 2 n_matmul + 4Ldt, or 2 n_matmul + 2Ldt when causal_avg (t is then the sequence length T), times 3 when train. For Llama-2-7B print 2 n_matmul = 13.21 GFLOP; the attention paid by one token at t = 512, 4,096 and 32,768 (0.27, 2.15, 17.18 GFLOP; 2.0%, 14.0%, 56.5% of that token's total); the causal average at T = 4,096 (1.07 GFLOP, +8.1% on the matrix multiplies); and the exact crossovers t = 25,205 and T = 50,410 beside the rule's 6d = 24,576 and 12d = 49,152.

Training FLOPs per token for Llama-2-7B at T = 4,096: 6 n_matmul + 6LdT = 39.64 + 3.22 = 42.87 GFLOP, beside the quick 6 N_total = 40.43 GFLOP (5.7% low). Exercise e13 multiplies by the training tokens.
Plot the parameter breakdown as stacked bars (fig-06-23) and FLOPs against context (fig-06-24).
expected_observations: The counter reproduces every published size exactly; the 12Ld^2 rule is within 1% for the multi-head 7B model but off by -11% to +55% for small models with GQA or wide FFNs.
Embeddings are a fifth to a third of a small model and under 4% of a 7B multi-head model.
Attention FLOPs are a rounding error at short context; for a single token they overtake the matrix multiplies beyond about 6d tokens of context, and averaged over a causal sequence beyond about 12d.
extensions: Add a mixture-of-experts option (E experts, top-k routing) and print total versus active parameters per token (concept in Module 05, engineering in Module 08).
Fetch the configuration of HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-360M with transformers.AutoConfig (a download of about 1 KB) and confirm 361,821,120 parameters.
Add a function for KV-cache bytes against context length and plot it for MHA, GQA-8 and MQA at the Llama-2-7B shape.

labs.title: Train a tiny GPT, sample from it, then remove the mask
labs.goal: Train the module's decoder at character level on a laptop CPU, confirm that the step-0 loss is log V, read the loss curve against reference entropies, sample and score the samples, then remove the causal mask and explain the curve that results.
labs.data: Generated by the lab: 12,000 seeded lines of a synthetic plant-maintenance log (486,841 characters, V = 46), split 90/10 into training and validation by position. No download.
steps: Set QUICK = True at the top: 300 causal steps and 200 without the mask, about 2 minutes on the prototype machine and about 3 on a laptop CPU. QUICK = False runs FULL_STEPS = 1,500 causal steps (a named constant) and the same 200 steps without the mask: about 5 minutes on the prototype machine (about 7 under load) and up to about 11 on a laptop, inside the 15-minute cap. Fix every seed: random.Random(0) for the corpus, torch.manual_seed(0) before building each model, torch.Generator seeds 1 (training batches), 2 (validation batches), 3 (sampling) and 5 (prefix-only evaluation).

Generate the corpus. For each of 12,000 lines draw, in this order, a letter from 'PTCHV', an identifier number 0-999 (printed with three digits) and a value from the letter's range: P pump pressure uniform 0.5-7.5 bar printed to one decimal (LOW below 2.0, HIGH above 6.0); T tank level integer 2-99 % (LOW below 10, HIGH above 90); C compressor speed integer 2,400-3,300 rpm (LOW below 2,600, HIGH above 3,100); H exchanger outlet integer 35-95 C (LOW below 40, HIGH above 85); V valve position integer 0-100 % (always OK). Write each line as 'P-104 pump pressure 4.2 bar OK end P-104'. Print the size (486,841 characters, 12,000 lines), V = 46 and the first three lines: 'H-776 exchanger outlet 91 C HIGH end H-776', 'H-041 exchanger outlet 51 C OK end H-041', 'V-497 valve position 51 % OK end V-497'.

Print reference levels in nats per character: log V = 3.829; unigram entropy 3.410 and bigram conditional entropy 1.717 (plug-in estimates from training-split counts); from the generator's own distribution, the true entropy 0.330 (13.39 nats per line over 40.57 characters per line: letter ln 5, three digits 3 ln 10, value 4.875 on average) and the floor for a model that cannot copy the closing identifier, 0.500 (20.30 nats per line).

Build the module's Decoder with vocab = 46, d = 128, 4 layers, 4 heads, 2 KV heads (d_ff = 341; 727,424 parameters) and a causal flag passed down to the attention's is_causal. First as written: print the loss on one batch, about 120 against log V = 3.83. Then add nn.init.normal_(model.emb.weight, std=0.02) and print it again: 3.884.

Train with AdamW (lr 3e-3, betas (0.9, 0.95), weight decay 0.1), a linear warmup over 50 steps then cosine decay to zero at the last step, gradient clipping at 1.0, batches of 32 random windows of 129 characters (128 inputs and 128 shifted targets). Print the training loss, the validation loss (mean of 10 batches) and the elapsed time at step 1 and every 100 steps, in both settings.

Sample 32 sequences of 240 characters at temperature 0.8, each starting from a newline, cropping the context to the last 128 characters, and print the first. Parse every complete line with ^([PTCHV])-(\d{3}) (\w+) (\w+) (\d+(?:\.\d)?) (\S+) (OK|LOW|HIGH) end ([PTCHV]-\d{3})$, require kind, quantity and unit to match the letter, and print three shares: well-formed lines; among them, lines whose closing identifier equals the opening one; and lines whose status is right for the value.

Remove the mask: rebuild with causal=False from the same seed and train 200 steps (in both settings) with the same optimiser and schedule; print the losses, sample once, and score both models on 200 prefix-only predictions from the validation split (a random window, a random prefix length 8-127, the next character scored from the last position only, which is what generation does).
Plot both training curves on a log step axis with horizontal lines at log V, the unigram and bigram entropies, 0.500 and 0.330 (fig-06-25).
expected_observations: QUICK, causal: step 1 train 3.884 / validation 3.855; step 100 0.558 / 0.567; step 200 0.551 / 0.545; step 300 0.532 / 0.536. The loss passes the unigram and bigram levels within 100 steps and flattens just above the 0.500 floor. Samples look right ('P-201 pump pressure 5.6 bar OK end P-828'), with the odd slip ('247r rpm'): 98.3% of 174 lines well-formed, statuses right for 87.1%, but the closing identifier copied in 0.0%: the model has learned the format and most of the status rule, and treats the closing identifier as random.

FULL, causal (1,500 steps): the plateau holds (0.565 / 0.572 at step 100, 0.539 / 0.531 at 500, 0.527 / 0.525 at 900), then the loss drops within about 200 steps: 0.504 / 0.508 at step 1,000, 0.425 / 0.418 at 1,100, 0.404 / 0.403 at 1,200, ending at 0.396 / 0.397 at 1,500. The drop is the model learning to copy the closing identifier from about 35 characters back, an induction-style mechanism (Lab 6): of 172 sampled lines 99.4% are well-formed, 98.2% close with their opening identifier and 99.4% have the right status ('P-201 pump pressure 5.6 bar OK end P-201'; the next line, 'C-143 compressor speed 3096 rpm OK end C-193', is one of the rare misses). The loss stays above the true 0.330 because the value distributions are not learned exactly. When the drop starts varies between machines: run on 2, 3, 6 and 8 threads instead of 4, the same schedule began its drop between steps 600 and 900 and still ended at 0.395-0.396 with 99-100% of identifiers copied. If a FULL run ends with the loss still between 0.50 and 0.40, the drop was under way when the learning rate ran out: set FULL_STEPS = 2,000 and rerun (about a third longer). The unmasked run is QUICK's 200 steps; prefix-only scoring gives 1.27 nats for the leaky model against 0.396 for the FULL causal model.

Without the mask (QUICK): step 50 0.976 / 0.906; step 100 0.274 / 0.261; step 150 0.027 / 0.024; step 200 0.018 / 0.019. The validation loss falls with the training loss because the leak is in the model, not the split. Samples are runs of one repeated letter; 2 of 53 lines parse, by chance. Scored from prefixes alone, the leaky model loses 1.27 nats per character against 0.53 for the causal model: it learned to read its answer, not to predict it. It still beats the bigram level (1.72) because the last position of every training window cannot see its target, so one position in 128 was trained honestly.

On the prototype machine (a desktop CPU limited to 4 threads, with other jobs running) a causal step took 160-350 ms depending on load; QUICK finished in 122 s end to end (183 ms per causal step), and FULL (1,500 + 200 steps) in about 5 minutes at 171 ms per causal step, which would be about 7 minutes at the 246 ms per step measured under heavier load. Expect up to about one and a half times longer on a laptop, about 11 minutes for FULL; the last digits of every loss may differ between machines, and so may the step at which FULL's drop begins.
extensions: Train on a plain-text file of your own (0.2-2 MB: notes, a public-domain book, a source file). Report log V, the unigram and bigram entropies, the final validation loss and a sample; then remove the mask and explain the curve.
Predict, then test: with a context window of 32 characters the closing identifier is about 35 characters after the opening one. What floor should the loss stop at, however long you train? (0.500.)
Sample at temperatures 0.3 and 1.5 and recount the three shares (decoding strategies are Module 07).

labs.title: Find an induction head
labs.goal: Train a two-layer attention-only transformer on sequences that repeat, watch the copying ability appear abruptly, identify the previous-token and induction heads by their attention, and confirm their role by ablation.
labs.data: Synthetic: sequences of 64 tokens over a 64-token vocabulary in which a random segment of random length 10-32 is immediately repeated (torch.Generator seeded 1; evaluation seeded 9 and 11).
steps: Generator: draw 64 random tokens; draw n uniformly from 10 to 32; overwrite positions n..2n-1 with positions 0..n-1; mark positions n+1..2n-1 as predictable (the first token of the copy cannot be predicted). Varying n stops the model from solving the task with a fixed positional offset.

Model: embedding (std 0.02), two layers of pre-RMSNorm multi-head attention (d = 64, 4 heads, RoPE, explicit softmax so the weights can be returned), no FFN, final RMSNorm, untied output layer. Write the attention by hand rather than with SDPA so that the weights are available.

Train 1,500 steps, batch 64, AdamW lr 1e-3, no weight decay; every 100 steps print the mean loss on predictable and on unpredictable positions. Expected: unpredictable stays at about 4.2-4.4 (ln 64 = 4.16); predictable falls slowly to 3.34 at step 500, then 2.68 at 600, 1.34 at 700, 0.79 at 800, 0.48 at 1,000 and 0.32 at 1,500.

Score every head on 256 fresh sequences: previous-token score = mean weight from t to t - 1; induction score = mean weight from a predictable position t to t - n + 1. Expected: layer 0 heads previous-token 0.04, 0.39, 0.20, 0.35 and induction about 0; layer 1 heads induction 0.88, 0.63, 0.89, 0.89.
Plot the attention pattern of the strongest previous-token head and the strongest induction head on one sequence (fig-06-8).

Ablation: zero one head's output before W_O and re-measure the predictable-position loss on 512 fresh sequences. Expected: baseline 0.34; zeroing any single layer-0 head 1.25-1.78; zeroing any single layer-1 head 0.75-1.95; zeroing all of layer 0 4.95 and all of layer 1 4.57, worse than guessing.

Control: retrain with one layer; the predictable-position loss stays near 3.3 (it learns that tokens seen earlier are likely to recur, not which one comes next) and no head's induction score exceeds 0.1.
expected_observations: The copying ability appears in a few hundred steps after a long plateau, the abrupt formation that Olsson et al. describe.
Two layers are necessary: the induction head in layer 1 needs the previous-token information that layer 0 writes into each position; one layer cannot do it.

Attention maps suggest the roles; the ablations confirm them. Every head of layer 0 matters, including the one whose previous-token score is low, which is a reminder that a single score is a summary, not an explanation.
extensions: Add SwiGLU FFNs and see whether the transition moves earlier or later.
Fix n = 32 for every sequence and show that a one-layer model now succeeds, because a fixed offset can be found by position alone.
Apply the induction score to the model trained in Lab 5 FULL mode, using the closing identifier of each line as the copied segment.

exercises.prompt: Under a causal mask the first position's attention output is exactly v_1, whatever Q and K are. Explain why, and say what this implies for the first position's next-token prediction in a decoder-only model.
exercises.solution_sketch: Row 1 has one unmasked score; the softmax of a single number is 1, so the output is v_1. Every layer behaves the same way at position 1, so the prediction made at position 1 depends only on the first token (and its position): the model is a bigram predictor there. The loss at position 1 therefore stays high, which is one reason the per-position loss falls with position.

exercises.prompt: Add a fourth token to the worked example of Section 3, with q_4 = k_4 = (1, -1), and remove the causal mask. Replace V by the 4 x 4 identity, so that each output row is that row's attention weights. Give the four rows to three decimals and interpret them: what does the new key do to rows 1-3, what weight does a key orthogonal to the query receive, and which rows would a causal mask have left exactly as in Section 3?
exercises.solution_sketch: Scaled scores Q K^T / sqrt(2): row 1 (0.707, 0, 0.707, 0.707); row 2 (0, 0.707, 0.707, -0.707); row 3 (0.707, 0.707, 1.414, 0); row 4 (0.707, -0.707, 0, 1.414). Only four exponentials occur: e^0.707 = 2.028, e^0 = 1, e^-0.707 = 0.493, e^1.414 = 4.113; the row sums are 7.084, 5.549, 9.169 and 7.634. Weights, which are the outputs because V = I: (0.286, 0.141, 0.286, 0.286); (0.180, 0.365, 0.365, 0.089); (0.221, 0.221, 0.449, 0.109); (0.266, 0.065, 0.131, 0.539). Without a mask every row gains a term in its denominator, so the first three tokens all change: token 3's weight on itself falls from 0.503 to 0.449. Key 4 is orthogonal to q_3 (score 0) and still receives 0.109: the softmax gives every visible key exp(score) > 0, so orthogonal does not mean ignored, and a negative score (row 4 on key 2, -0.707) only means a small weight (0.065). With the causal mask, rows 1-3 would be exactly those of Section 3, because no earlier row can see token 4; only row 4 would be new. With identity values the output is the attention map itself, which is what attention plots show.

exercises.prompt: In the soft lookup of Section 1 the scaled weights are (0.248, 0.248, 0.503); without the 1/sqrt(d_k) factor they become (0.212, 0.212, 0.576). Describe what happens to the weights of a typical row at d_k = 128 with unit-variance queries and keys, and why this slows the learning of W_Q and W_K.
exercises.solution_sketch: The scores have standard deviation sqrt(128) = 11.3, so typical gaps between scores are around 10 and the softmax is nearly one-hot (median largest weight 0.978 over 16 keys). The Jacobian diag(p) - p p^T is then nearly zero (J_11 = 2.5e-5 for scores (11.3, 0, 0)), so dL/ds and hence the gradients reaching W_Q and W_K are tiny; the model starts with an almost fixed, arbitrary attention pattern and learns to change it slowly.

exercises.prompt: Let P be a T x T permutation matrix. (a) Show that unmasked self-attention without position information is permutation-equivariant: Attention(PX) = P Attention(X). (b) Show that permuting keys and values together, but not the queries, leaves the output unchanged. (c) Does (a) still hold with a causal mask? Conclude why position must be injected.
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) Q' = PXW_Q = PQ, K' = PK, V' = PV; S' = P Q K^T P^T / sqrt(d_k) = P S P^T. A row-wise softmax commutes with permuting rows, and with permuting the columns of every row by the same permutation, so softmax(P S P^T) = P softmax(S) P^T; the output is P softmax(S) P^T P V = P softmax(S) V, using P^T P = I. (b) softmax(S P^T) P V = softmax(S) P^T P V = softmax(S) V. (c) No: the mask depends on position, so permuting the input changes which keys each query may see; a causal model can infer some position from how many tokens it sees. Without a mask the model treats its input as a set, so 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' produce the same outputs in permuted order.

exercises.prompt: Write the residual update of a pre-norm and of a post-norm block. In which is there an unbroken identity path from the embedding to the last layer, and what does that imply for the gradient at initialisation?
exercises.solution_sketch: Pre-norm: x <- x + F(Norm(x)). Post-norm: x <- Norm(x + F(x)). Pre-norm has the identity path: x_L = x_0 + sum_l F_l(Norm(x_l)), so dx_L/dx_l = I + (terms through the layers), and the gradient reaches every layer at least through the identity. In post-norm each Norm's Jacobian sits on the path, so gradients are rescaled L times; at initialisation those near the output are large (Xiong et al. 2020), which is why post-norm needs warmup.

exercises.prompt: Section 6 proved in complex form that one RoPE pair contributes a score depending only on t - s. (a) Write R_t, the d_k x d_k block-diagonal matrix of 2 x 2 rotations by t theta_i, and prove R_t^T R_s = R_{s-t}, hence (R_t q)^T (R_s k) = q^T R_{s-t} k. (b) Show that RoPE preserves vector norms. (c) Show that rotating the values too would make the attention output depend on absolute position.
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) Each block is R(t theta_i) = [[cos, -sin], [sin, cos]]; R(a)^T = R(-a) and R(a)R(b) = R(a + b), so block by block R(t theta_i)^T R(s theta_i) = R((s - t) theta_i); then (R_t q)^T (R_s k) = q^T R_t^T R_s k = q^T R_{s-t} k, a function of q, k and s - t only. (b) R_t is orthogonal: ||R_t q||^2 = q^T R_t^T R_t q = q^T q. (c) The output at t would be sum_s p_ts R_s v_s: each value carries the rotation of its absolute position s, so the same content at shifted positions gives differently rotated vectors and the downstream layers see absolute position.

exercises.prompt: A model trained with learned absolute position embeddings for 1,024 positions is given a 2,000-token input. What happens? Why does a RoPE model degrade more gracefully, and why does it still degrade?
exercises.solution_sketch: Positions 1,024 and beyond have no embedding row (an index error) or, if the table is larger, untrained vectors; the model has no meaningful input for them. RoPE defines a rotation for every position and the score depends only on t - s, so every relative offset up to 1,023 was seen in training; offsets beyond that put the slow pairs at angles never seen, and quality falls (Section 6, context extension).

exercises.prompt: BERT is trained to fill in masked tokens with bidirectional attention. Give two reasons it cannot be used as it stands to generate text left to right.
exercises.solution_sketch: It was never trained to predict the next token from a prefix: during training it always had context on both sides, and at generation time the right-hand context does not exist. Its loss covered only the 15% of selected positions, so its outputs elsewhere are not trained next-token distributions. (Also, with no causal mask, every generated token would change every earlier representation, so each step re-encodes the whole sequence.)

exercises.prompt: Llama-3-8B has 32 query heads and 8 key-value heads with head dimension 128 at d = 4,096. Compared with a multi-head version of the same model, which weight matrices are smaller and by what factor, and which inference-time tensor shrinks by the same factor? Which costs do not change?
exercises.solution_sketch: W_K and W_V map d = 4,096 to n_kv d_head = 1,024 dimensions instead of 4,096, so each is a quarter of its multi-head size; W_Q, W_O and the FFN are unchanged. The KV cache per token shrinks by the same factor of 4 (Section 9: from 524,288 B (512 KiB) to 131,072 B (128 KiB) in bf16 at L = 32). The FLOPs of Q K^T and P V do not change, because every query head still attends over every key, and neither do those of W_Q, W_O and the FFN.

exercises.prompt: FlashAttention and sliding-window attention both reduce the memory of attention. Explain in one sentence each why one of them leaves the model's outputs unchanged and the other does not, and what that means for using each with an existing trained model.
exercises.solution_sketch: FlashAttention computes exactly the same softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d_k))V in a different order (tiles with running maxima and sums), so outputs agree to rounding and it can replace the standard kernel in any trained model. Sliding-window attention masks keys further back than w, which changes the function itself, so a model must be trained (or at least fine-tuned) with the window it will be served with.

exercises.prompt: Online softmax by hand: process scores s = (2, 1, 3, 0) with scalar values v = (1, 2, 3, 4) in two blocks of two. Write m, l and the unnormalised accumulator a after each block, give the output a / l, and check it against the direct softmax-weighted average.

Count the parameters of the module's Decoder (vocab = 4,096, d = 256, 4 layers, 8 heads, 2 KV heads, d_ff = int(8 x 256 / 3), tied embeddings, RMSNorm with a weight and no bias) by hand: embeddings, per-layer attention, per-layer FFN, norms, final norm. Compare with the printed number and with 12Ld^2, and explain the difference.
exercises.solution_sketch: Embeddings 4,096 x 256 = 1,048,576 (counted once: tied). d_k = 32, KV width 2 x 32 = 64. Attention: wq 65,536 + wk 16,384 + wv 16,384 + wo 65,536 = 163,840. d_ff = 682; FFN 3 x 256 x 682 = 523,776. Norms 2 x 256 = 512. Per layer 688,128; four layers 2,752,512; final norm 256. Total 3,801,344, as printed. 12Ld^2 = 3,145,728 assumes full multi-head attention (4d^2 = 262,144 per layer) and an FFN of exactly 8d^2 = 524,288: GQA saves 98,304 per layer and the rounding of 682.7 down to 682 saves 512; the norms add 512 per layer; the embeddings add 1,048,576.

exercises.prompt: Llama 2 7B (N_total = 6,738,415,616 parameters, of which the untied input embedding is V d = 131,072,000; L = 32, d = 4,096) was pretrained on 2.0 trillion tokens in sequences of 4,096; its paper reports 184,320 A100 GPU-hours for this model. (a) Estimate the training compute twice: with the quick C = 6 N_total D, and with Section 11's convention, C = (6 N_matmul + 6LdT) D. (b) Turn each into a sustained FLOP/s per GPU and a fraction of the A100's dense bf16 peak of 312 TFLOP/s (NVIDIA's specification). (c) Why does the quick estimate land close, and what does even the convention leave out?
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) Quick: 6 x 6.738e9 x 2.0e12 = 8.09e22 FLOPs. Convention: N_matmul = 6,607,343,616, so 6 N_matmul D = 7.93e22; causal attention 6LdT D = 6 x 32 x 4,096 x 4,096 x 2.0e12 = 6.44e21, 8.1% on top of the matrix multiplies; C = 8.57e22. (b) GPU-seconds 184,320 x 3,600 = 6.64e8; 8.09e22 / 6.64e8 = 1.22e14 FLOP/s per GPU, 39% of peak; 8.57e22 / 6.64e8 = 1.29e14 FLOP/s, 41%. (c) The quick form counts the input embedding, which costs no FLOPs (1.6e21), and omits attention (6.4e21); the two errors partly cancel and it lands 5.7% low. Attention adds about 8%, not 16%: 16% is what the last token of a 4,096-token context pays, or what a kernel that also computes the masked half would spend (utilisation would then come out at about 45%). Neither form counts recomputed activations, evaluation, restarts or lost steps, which used GPU-hours without adding model FLOPs, so the arithmetic units were busier than 41% while the job ran. Module 08 plans H100 runs at an assumed 40% (4e14 FLOP/s sustained), the same order.

exercises.prompt: A colleague's character-level causal transformer reaches a training loss of 0.02 nats per character after 150 steps, and the validation loss is just as low. Name two bugs that produce exactly this, and one check that separates a real model from a leak.
exercises.solution_sketch: A missing or wrong causal mask (is_causal=False, a mask of the wrong orientation), or a target that is not shifted (targets equal inputs, or the input includes the target). Checks: generate text (a leak generates garbage); score each next character from its prefix alone (Lab 5: 1.27 nats for the leaky model against 0.53 for the causal one); or change token t + 1 and confirm the logits at t do not move. The validation loss cannot tell, because the leak is in the model, not the split.

exercises.prompt: Replace F.scaled_dot_product_attention in the module's Attention class by an explicit implementation that builds the (B, h, T, T) score matrix, masks the upper triangle with -inf and applies the softmax. (a) Check that the outputs agree with the fused call to within 1e-5. (b) With B = 1, h = 8, d_k = 64 in float32, time both versions at T = 512, 2,048 and 4,096 on your machine and compute the size of the score matrix at each T. (c) On a GPU (Colab), measure torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated for both at T = 512, 2,048 and 8,192. Then restore the fused call.
exercises.solution_sketch: Explicit: s = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / sqrt(d_k); s = s.masked_fill(torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T, dtype=torch.bool), 1), float('-inf')); y = s.softmax(-1) @ v. Maximum difference about 6e-7. Score matrix B h T^2 x 4 bytes: 8 MiB, 128 MiB, 512 MiB (and 2 GiB at 8,192). On the prototype CPU (4 threads) the explicit version took about 0.009, 0.11 and 0.50 s against 0.003, 0.014 and 0.048 s fused; the explicit time grows roughly as T^2 and is dominated by writing and reading the score matrix. On a GPU the explicit version's peak memory grows as T^2 (gigabytes at 8,192) while the fused kernel's stays nearly linear in T, which is the point of Section 10. Expect different absolute times on your hardware.

quiz.question: For a batch of B sequences of length T with h heads of width d_k, what is the shape of the attention-weight tensor?
options: (B, T, d)
(B, h, T, d_k)
(B, h, T, T)
(B, T, T, h)
quiz.explanation: Each head scores every query position against every key position, giving a T x T matrix per head per sequence: (B, h, T, T). (B, h, T, d_k) is the shape of q, k, v and the per-head output; (B, T, d) is the shape entering and leaving the layer; (B, T, T, h) is a legal layout but not the one the code produces.

quiz.question: Why are the scores divided by sqrt(d_k)?
options: To keep the scores at roughly unit variance, so the softmax does not saturate and its gradient does not vanish at initialisation
To make each row of attention weights sum to one
To reduce the number of FLOPs in Q K^T
To make attention independent of the sequence length
quiz.explanation: With independent unit-variance entries, q.k has variance d_k; dividing by sqrt(d_k) restores variance 1. The softmax already makes rows sum to one, the division adds FLOPs rather than removing them, and it has nothing to do with T.

quiz.question: Under a causal mask, what is the attention weight of position 3 on position 5?
options: A small positive number that training drives towards zero
Exactly zero
Equal to the weight of position 5 on position 3
quiz.explanation: The score is set to -inf before the softmax, and exp(-inf) = 0 exactly. Nothing is learned about it; the future is structurally invisible. Attention is not symmetric, and 1/T is the uniform weight without a mask.

quiz.question: An unmasked transformer layer with no positional encoding receives a sentence, and then the same sentence with its tokens shuffled. How do the two sets of output vectors compare?
options: Identical, in the same order
Entirely different
The same vectors, shuffled in the same way as the input
They differ only by a scale factor
quiz.explanation: Self-attention without position is permutation-equivariant: Attention(PX) = P Attention(X). The model sees a set, which is why order must be injected. The outputs are not in the original order, nor different vectors.

quiz.question: Which tensors does RoPE rotate?
options: The token embeddings, once, at the input
Queries, keys and values
Only the attention output
Queries and keys, in every attention layer
quiz.explanation: RoPE rotates q and k so that their dot product depends only on t - s; values are untouched, and the rotation is applied inside every layer. Adding a vector at the input is what sinusoidal and learned absolute encodings do.

quiz.question: A decoder has L = 32 layers of width d = 4,096 with multi-head attention and an FFN of 8d^2 parameters. About how many parameters are in its layers, excluding embeddings?
options: 0.5 billion
6.4 billion
2.1 billion
12.9 billion
quiz.explanation: 12 L d^2 = 12 x 32 x 4,096^2 = 6.44e9: 4d^2 for attention and 8d^2 for the FFN per layer. 2.1B counts only the attention (4 L d^2); 12.9B counts every layer twice; 0.5B would need a width of about 1,100 at the same depth.

quiz.question: For a dense decoder at short context, with N_matmul parameters in its matrix multiplies, the forward pass costs about how many FLOPs per token, and a training step about how many per token?
options: 2 N_matmul and 6 N_matmul
N_matmul and 3 N_matmul
2 N_matmul and 4 N_matmul
6 N_matmul and 18 N_matmul
quiz.explanation: Each such weight takes part in one multiply-add per token in the forward pass (2 FLOPs); the backward pass computes two products of the same size per layer (gradients with respect to inputs and weights), so training costs three times the forward pass. At long context add attention, 4Ldt per token at context t (2LdT averaged over a causal sequence), also times three for training.

quiz.question: Compared with multi-head attention, grouped-query attention with 32 query heads and 8 key-value heads reduces:
options: The number of query heads to 8
The FLOPs of Q K^T by a factor of 4
The FFN width
The KV cache and the K and V projection weights by a factor of 4
quiz.explanation: Groups of four query heads share one KV head, so K and V projections and the cache shrink four-fold. All 32 query heads remain and each still scores every key, so the FLOPs of Q K^T are unchanged; the FFN is unaffected.

quiz.question: How does FlashAttention reduce attention's memory from O(T^2) to O(T)?
options: By approximating the softmax with a low-rank kernel
By computing attention tile by tile with a running maximum and running sum, so the T x T matrix is never stored
By restricting each query to a sliding window of keys
By storing scores in 8-bit integers
quiz.explanation: The online softmax lets each tile be folded into running statistics and an output accumulator, then discarded; the result is exact. Low-rank kernels and sliding windows change the function; quantising scores would reduce memory by a constant, not change its order.

quiz.question: A character-level model with V = 46 reports a loss of 3.88 at step 0. What does this indicate?
options: The model is broken: the loss at initialisation should be near zero
The model has already learned the bigram statistics
The initial logits are nearly uniform, as they should be: ln 46 = 3.83
The learning rate is too high
quiz.explanation: A model that knows nothing should spread its probability evenly, giving a cross-entropy of log V; small random logits add a little (about sigma^2/2). The bigram entropy of that corpus is 1.72, so nothing has been learned yet; no training step has happened for the learning rate to matter.

quiz.question: Which statement about pre-norm transformers is correct?
options: The normalisation is applied after the residual addition
They make residual connections unnecessary
Their residual path from input to output contains no normalisation, so gradients reach every layer directly, and they train stably without a long warmup
They double the number of normalisation parameters
quiz.explanation: Pre-norm normalises the input of each sublayer, x + F(Norm(x)), leaving an identity path. Normalising after the addition is post-norm. Residuals are essential to both; the parameter count of the norms is the same.

quiz.question: Which is the best summary of why the decoder-only shape became the default for large language models?
options: Every token is a training target, one next-token objective covers every task written as text, and generation is the product
It has the lowest cost per token of the three shapes at any size
Encoders cannot be scaled beyond a billion parameters
Cross-attention cannot be implemented with FlashAttention
quiz.explanation: The reasons are training signal, generality and the product. Costs per token are similar across shapes at equal size; encoders scale fine; fused kernels handle cross-attention.

widgets.name: attention-calculator
widgets.teaching_point: Each row of softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) is a probability distribution over the keys a query may see, and the output row is the matching mixture of value rows; the mask zeroes the future exactly and the scale sets how sharp the lookup is.
controls: editable number grids for Q (T x d_k), K (T x d_k) and V (T x d_v): numeric inputs, step 0.1, clamped to [-10, 10]; preloaded with the worked example
segmented buttons: T = 2, 3 or 4 tokens; d_k = d_v = 1, 2, 3 or 4 (resizing keeps existing cells and fills new ones with 0)
slider: sharpness multiplier c applied to the scores, 0.1 to 20, logarithmic, default 1
preset buttons: 'worked example', 'unmasked', 'unscaled', 'V = identity' (sets d_v = T and V = I), 'hard lookup' (c = 20), 'reset'
row selector: click a row of the weight heat map, or use the arrow keys, to choose the query row (default row 3)
displays: the raw score matrix QK^T and the scaled matrix c QK^T / sqrt(d_k), masked cells shown as '-inf' on a grey background
the weight matrix P as a heat map (one hue, light to dark for 0 to 1), each cell labelled to three decimals, with each row's sum (1.000) beside it
the output matrix O = P V, three decimals

for the selected row when d_v = 2: a 2D plot of the value rows as labelled points, the convex hull of the visible ones shaded, the output as a hollow marker, and a line from each visible value to the output with width proportional to its weight; when d_v is not 2, a bar chart of the row's weights instead
for the selected row: the largest weight, the entropy in nats beside log(number of visible keys), and a 'saturated' badge when the largest weight exceeds 0.99

with 'show gradient' on: the row's Jacobian diag(p) - p p^T over the visible keys as a small table, and dL/ds for L = the last component of the selected output row, with the sum of dL/ds (always 0.000)
widgets.defaults: The worked example: Q = K = [[1,0],[0,1],[1,1]], V = [[1,0],[0,2],[3,3]], causal on, scaling on, c = 1, row 3 selected. On load the reader sees P row 3 = (0.248, 0.248, 0.503) and O row 3 = (1.759, 2.007) as a point inside the triangle of values, exactly the numbers of Section 3.
widgets.spec: Compute in double precision. S = Q K^T (T x T); if scaling, divide by sqrt(d_k); multiply by c; if causal, S_ij = -Infinity for j > i. Row-wise safe softmax: m_i = max of the unmasked S_ij; P_ij = exp(S_ij - m_i) / sum over unmasked j of exp(S_ij - m_i); P_ij = 0 where masked. O = P V. A causal row always keeps its diagonal and an unmasked row keeps everything, so no row is ever empty. Display numbers with toFixed(3) and masked scores as '-inf'. Inputs: parse with Number(); if the result is NaN or the field is empty, restore the previous value; clamp to [-10, 10]. Resizing keeps the top-left block. 'V = identity' sets d_v = T and V = I_T and leaves d_k alone. Gradient panel for selected row i: g_j = V[j][d_v - 1] (because L = O[i][d_v - 1]); dL/ds_ij = P_ij (g_j - sum_k P_ik g_k) for visible j; Jacobian entries P_ij (delta_jk - P_ik). Test values to hard-code in a self-check: with the defaults, row 2 = (0.330, 0.670, 0), O row 2 = (0.330, 1.340); unmasked row 1 = (0.401, 0.198, 0.401); unscaled row 3 = (0.212, 0.212, 0.576); gradient on with row 3 selected: dL/ds = (-0.498, -0.002, 0.500). Heat-map colour: interpolate from the page background (weight 0) to a strong tone of one hue (weight 1) using theme tokens for light and dark themes; switch the label colour above weight 0.6 for contrast. Every control is keyboard-operable with a visible focus ring; grid inputs carry labels such as 'Q row 2, column 1' for screen readers. Vanilla JavaScript and SVG, no libraries; recompute and redraw everything on each input event (the computation is tiny). Below 600 px wide, stack the matrices vertically; nothing may require horizontal scrolling of the page except the matrices' own container.

widgets.name: rope-explorer
widgets.teaching_point: RoPE rotates each two-dimensional pair of q and k by an angle proportional to position, at frequencies that fall geometrically across the pairs, so the score depends only on t - s; fast pairs wrap within a few tokens while slow pairs barely turn inside the training context, which is where context-extension methods intervene.
controls: slider: query position t, 0 to 4,096, integer
slider: key position s, 0 to 4,096, integer
checkbox: lock offset (moving t moves s by the same amount, keeping t - s fixed); default off
select: head dimension d_k in {8, 16, 64, 128}; default 128
select: vectors 'q = k = all ones' (default), 'q = (1,0,1,0,...), k = (0,1,0,1,...)', 'random (seed 1)'
select: extension 'none' (default), 'position interpolation', 'NTK-aware base', with a slider for the extension factor kappa from 1 to 8 (default 4), enabled when an extension is chosen
number input: training context length, default 4,096 (used to shade the wavelength chart)
displays: a grid of small dials, one per pair i = 0 .. d_k/2 - 1 (64 dials in rows of 16 at d_k = 128), each showing the q-pair arrow at angle t theta_i, the k-pair arrow at angle s theta_i and the angle between them
a line chart of the normalised score against the offset Delta = t - s from 0 to 4,096 (a toggle switches to a log x-axis from 1 to 16,384), with a marker at the current offset
a readout: score(t, s), score(t + 100, s + 100) and their difference (0.000 at display precision)

a bar chart of log10 of the wavelength 2 pi / theta_i for every pair, with a horizontal line at the training context; bars above the line shaded and labelled 'never completes a rotation in training'; when an extension is active, ghost bars show the original wavelengths
widgets.defaults: d_k = 128, base 10,000, q = k = all ones, t = 10, s = 3, no extension, training context 4,096. The curve starts at 1.0, reads 0.970 at offset 1, 0.620 at 16 and about 0.2 by 1,024; the readout shows equal scores for (10, 3) and (110, 103); 18 of the 64 bars are shaded.
widgets.spec: theta_i = base^(-2i/d_k) for i = 0 .. d_k/2 - 1. With 'position interpolation' use positions t/kappa and s/kappa (fractions allowed) and the original base; with 'NTK-aware base' use base' = base x kappa^(d_k/(d_k - 2)) and the original positions. For each pair let a_i = q_{2i} k_{2i} + q_{2i+1} k_{2i+1} and b_i = q_{2i+1} k_{2i} - q_{2i} k_{2i+1}; the score at offset Delta is sum_i [a_i cos(Delta theta_i) - b_i sin(Delta theta_i)], equal to the dot product of the rotated vectors (state the derivation from Re(z_q conj(z_k) exp(i Delta theta)) in a code comment). Normalise the plotted score by sum_i sqrt((q_{2i}^2 + q_{2i+1}^2)(k_{2i}^2 + k_{2i+1}^2)) so it lies in [-1, 1]; show the raw score in the readout as well. Evaluate the curve at every integer offset 0 .. 4,096 (or 200 log-spaced offsets for the log axis): at most about 262,000 cosines per redraw. Self-check values with the defaults: normalised score 0.970 at offset 1, 0.620 at 16, 0.333 at 128; NTK base for kappa = 4 at d_k = 128 is 40,890; with q = (1,0,...), k = (0,1,...) and d_k = 2, base irrelevant (theta_0 = 1), score(3, 1) = sin 2 = 0.909. 'random (seed 1)' uses a mulberry32 generator seeded 1 with Box-Muller normals, regenerated when d_k changes. Dials are SVG circles with two arrows in two theme colours; draw them larger at d_k = 8 or 16. Wavelength axis: log10 from 0 to 7. With lock offset on, clamp both positions to [0, 4,096] when the pair would leave it. Theme-aware colours; sliders keyboard-operable with aria-valuetext; below 600 px wide the panels stack. Vanilla JavaScript; SVG for dials and bars, canvas or SVG for the curve.
